SYNTHETIC TEST MATERIAL
BIOLOGY 10 - Fall 2026
Riverbend High School, Room 214
Instructor: Ms. Dana Okafor-Lindqvist, email dokafor@riverbend.example
Meets: Mon/Wed/Fri, Period 3. Lab days are usually Wednesdays.
Office hours: Tuesdays 3:15-4:00 PM or by appointment.

COURSE DESCRIPTION
This course covers the basics of life science: cells, energy, cell division, genetics, evolution, and ecology. Students do weekly labs and a short written lab report each unit.

WEEKLY SCHEDULE
Week 1 (Aug 24): Intro, lab safety, scientific method
Week 2 (Aug 31): Characteristics of life, biochemistry basics
Week 3 (Sep 7): Macromolecules (no school Mon Sep 7, Labor Day)
Week 4 (Sep 14): Cell structure, organelles. Quiz 1 on Fri Sep 11 covers macromolecules.
Week 5 (Sep 21): Cell membrane, diffusion, osmosis
Week 6 (Sep 28): Enzymes. Quiz 2 on Fri Oct 2: cell structure and membrane transport.
Week 7 (Oct 5): Photosynthesis
Week 8 (Oct 12): Cellular respiration
Week 9 (Oct 19): Cell cycle, mitosis, meiosis. Quiz 3 on Fri Oct 23: photosynthesis and cellular respiration.
Week 10 (Oct 26): Review week. Unit Test (midterm) on Fri Oct 30: Units 1-3, cells and energy.
Week 11 (Nov 2): Mendel and heredity, Punnett squares
Week 12 (Nov 9): DNA structure and replication. Quiz 4 on Fri Nov 13: mitosis, meiosis, and Punnett squares.
Week 13 (Nov 16): Protein synthesis, mutations
Week 14 (Nov 23): Short week, no school Nov 25-27 (Thanksgiving break)
Week 15 (Nov 30): Evolution and natural selection. Quiz 5 on Fri Dec 4: DNA, protein synthesis, mutations.
Week 16 (Dec 7): Ecology, food webs, energy flow
Week 17 (Dec 14): Final review. Final Exam on Wed Dec 16, Period 3, cumulative.

ASSESSMENTS
Quizzes: five quizzes, 20-25 minutes each, mix of multiple choice and short answer. The lowest quiz score is dropped only if all five are taken.
Unit Test (midterm): Fri Oct 30, 50 minutes.
Final Exam: Wed Dec 16, 90 minutes, covers the whole course with extra weight on Units 4-6.
Lab reports: four reports due about one week after each lab unit.

GRADING BREAKDOWN
Quizzes: 20%
Unit Test (midterm): 20%
Final Exam: 25%
Lab reports: 20%
Homework and classwork: 10%
Participation: 5%

Grade scale: A 90-100, B 80-89, C 70-79, D 60-69, F below 60.

POLICIES
1. Late work: Homework and lab reports lose 10% per day late, up to 3 days. After 3 days they are not accepted unless there is an excused absence.
2. Make-up quizzes and tests: If you miss an assessment with an excused absence, you must make it up within 5 school days, during lunch or after school in Room 214. Tell Ms. Okafor-Lindqvist ahead of time if you can.
3. Academic honesty and phones: Phones stay in the classroom phone caddy during quizzes and tests. Copying lab data or using AI to write lab reports counts as cheating and gets a zero plus a call home.

MATERIALS
Bring a binder, pencils, a scientific calculator for some labs, and the textbook Biology: Living Systems (class set stays in the room). Dates may change with notice from the instructor, so check the class page and write changes in your planner.
notes:
BIO NOTES - Aiden

TOPIC 1: MITOSIS (cell division for growth + repair)
- cell cycle = interphase (G1, S, G2) then M phase then cytokinesis
- interphase is the LONGEST part, cell grows + copies DNA in S phase (S = synthesis)
- PMAT = prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
  * prophase: chromatin condenses -> chromosomes, nuclear envelope breaks down, spindle forms
  * metaphase: chromosomes line up in the MIDDLE (metaphase plate) - M = middle
  * anaphase: sister chromatids pulled APART to opposite sides - A = apart
  * telophase: 2 new nuclei form, chromosomes unwind, basically prophase backwards
- cytokinesis: cytoplasm splits. animal cells = pinch (cleavage furrow), plant cells = cell plate
- result: 2 identical daughter cells, diploid (2n), same # chromosomes as parent
- humans 2n = 46
- cancer = cells dividing w/o control, checkpoints fail (G1 checkpoint, G2, M)
- Q to ask: is the centromere the same as the centrosome?? (NO - centromere holds chromatids together, centrosome makes spindle fibers. ask Ms O to confirm)

TOPIC 2: CELL MEMBRANE + TRANSPORT
- phospholipid bilayer, heads = hydrophilic (love water), tails = hydrophobic
- fluid mosaic model - proteins float in the lipid layer like a mosaic
- selectively permeable = lets some stuff thru, not all
- PASSIVE transport = no energy (ATP) needed, goes high -> low conc (down the gradient)
  * diffusion: ex O2, CO2 just move across
  * facilitated diffusion: needs channel/carrier protein, ex glucose
  * osmosis: diffusion of WATER across membrane
- ACTIVE transport = needs ATP, goes low -> high (against gradient), ex sodium-potassium pump
- endocytosis = cell takes stuff IN w/ vesicle, exocytosis = pushes stuff OUT
- tonicity:
  * hypotonic sol = less solute outside, water goes IN, animal cell may burst (lysis)
  * hypertonic = more solute outside, water goes OUT, cell shrinks (plant = plasmolysis)
  * isotonic = equal, no net movement
- lab: potato cores in salt water, the ones in high salt lost mass. makes sense bc hypertonic!!

TO STUDY: PMAT order, tonicity examples, passive vs active chart. Quiz soon!!

So, first thing. What is meiosis for? Anybody? Yeah, Priya, exactly, it makes gametes. Sex cells. Sperm and egg in humans. And, um, the big deal is that gametes have half the number of chromosomes. So our body cells are diploid, that's two n, forty-six chromosomes in humans, and the gametes are haploid, that's n, twenty-three. So if we didn't halve it, then, you know, every generation would double the chromosome number and, um, that would be a real problem.

So meiosis has two rounds of division. Meiosis one and meiosis two. And, so, before it even starts, the cell goes through interphase and copies its DNA, just like in mitosis, so you start with each chromosome made of two sister chromatids. Okay? Only one round of copying but two rounds of dividing. That's the trick, and this will be on the exam.

Now in meiosis one, the homologous chromosomes pair up. Homologous means, um, same genes, same size, one from mom and one from dad. They pair up in prophase one and they swap pieces. That is called crossing over. And this is super important because it mixes up the genes, so, so, the gametes end up genetically different from each other and from the parent. In mitosis you get clones. In meiosis you get variety.

Then in metaphase one, the pairs line up in the middle, and in anaphase one the homologous pairs are pulled apart. Not the sister chromatids, the homologous pairs. That's the part people always get wrong. After meiosis one you have two cells and each one is haploid, but each chromosome still has two chromatids.

Oh, by the way, before I forget, my dog got into the compost pile this weekend and I spent an hour giving him a bath. Anyway, sorry, back to it. Not important. Okay.

Meiosis two looks a lot like mitosis. The chromosomes line up, and this time the sister chromatids are pulled apart. So when you're done you have four cells, each haploid, each genetically different. Four cells, not two. Write that down. Mitosis gives two identical diploid cells, meiosis gives four different haploid cells.

So, um, one more thing, independent assortment. When the pairs line up in metaphase one, they line up randomly. Which side the mom chromosome goes on is basically a coin flip for each pair. With twenty-three pairs in humans that's over eight million combinations, even before crossing over. So you and your sibling are different, um, that's why.

And what happens if it goes wrong? If the chromosomes don't separate properly, that's called nondisjunction. You can get a gamete with an extra or a missing chromosome. Down syndrome is trisomy twenty-one, so three copies of chromosome twenty-one. We'll look at a karyotype tomorrow.
